text: Every December, hundreds of thousands of cars drive home from Germany and Austria to Romania. Before the border, everyone asks the same thing: what do I need to buy?
The answer is spread over four toll operators, four languages and a lot of old blog posts. And this year it changed. Romania rewrote its vignette on the first of October.
This is Drum Bun. Brașov to Munich on the twentieth of December, back on the third of January, in a Euro 5 diesel.
The planner walks the route stored in Sanity: every road section, the products that cover it, and the price valid on each day you drive.
In Austria, two one-day vignettes beat a ten-day one, because the drive home is two weeks later. The 2027 prices aren't published yet, and it says so.
In Romania the price now depends on the Euro class. A Euro 5 diesel pays 26 lei a day. Without a known class, you pay the Euro 0 rate.
Before you go: winter tyres in three countries, and in Germany M plus S no longer counts. Munich needs a green sticker, and this car qualifies.
And the claims you probably read online, each linked to the fact that corrects it.
You can also ask the agent, in Romanian, German, Hungarian or English. Here it plans a trip in Romanian.
It runs the same planner, reads the Knowledge Base through Sanity Context, and shows every step it took.
The Knowledge Base is built from official pages in four languages, plus the blogs drivers actually read.
When sources disagree, the build files an issue. I resolved them in code, and each decision becomes a standing rule for the next build.
It caught mistakes in my own data model. And when a ministry page still quoted an old fine, it flagged that too.
Against keyword search over the same content, the agent gets fifteen of sixteen test questions right. Search gets eleven. It finds the documents, but it can't compute a trip.
Drum Bun. Structured content in Sanity, so the answer is computed, not guessed. Drum bun!
